summary: Defines the ENABLE command for IMAP. Most IMAP extensions can simply be used if the server supports them, but a few change server behavior and so need the client to opt in. ENABLE lets a client tell the server which of those extensions it understands. It is a standards-track specification.

plainLanguage.summary: IMAP is the protocol a mail client uses to read mail from a server. Some extensions let the server push extra information to the client without being asked, and the server has to be sure the client can read it. This RFC adds a command where the client lists the extensions it understands, and the server turns them on.

how does an imap client opt in to an extension
subtitle: An IMAP command that lets a client tell the server which extensions it understands.

tldr.problem: Some IMAP extensions let the server send unsolicited data back, but the server cannot send it until it knows the client will understand it.
tldr.mechanism: A new ENABLE command takes a list of extension names. The server turns on the ones it supports and answers with an untagged ENABLED response listing what it enabled.
tldr.outcome: Extensions can now be switched on explicitly instead of by side effect. At the time of writing, CONDSTORE was the only extension that used it, and the RFC discourages new extensions from needing it.

facts.label: When the command may be sent
facts.value: Authenticated state, before any mailbox is selected

today: RFC 5161 is a Proposed Standard from March 2008, and the unit metadata lists no RFC that obsoletes or updates it. The word ENABLE was added to the IMAP4 capabilities registry, so a server that supports it says so in its capability list.

sections.title: Why a Client Needs to Say What It Supports
sections.content:
Several IMAP extensions allow the server to return unsolicited responses specific to those extensions in certain circumstances. However, servers cannot send those unsolicited responses until they know that the clients support such extensions and thus will not choke on the extension response data.

Until now, extensions have typically stated that a server cannot send the unsolicited responses until after the client has used a command with the extension data, at which point the server knows the client is aware of the extension. CONDSTORE, ANNOTATE and some extensions under consideration at the time use various commands to enable server extensions. For example, CONDSTORE uses a SELECT or FETCH parameter, and ANNOTATE uses a side effect of FETCH.

The ENABLE extension provides an explicit indication from the client that it supports particular extensions, using a new ENABLE command. An IMAP server that supports ENABLE advertises this by including the word ENABLE in its capability list. Most IMAP extensions do not require the client to enable the extension in any way.
sections.plainLanguage: Some extensions let the server volunteer information the client did not ask for. Sending that to a client that does not understand it would break the session. Before this RFC, the only way to find out was for the client to use the extension first and for the server to notice. This RFC makes the client say so up front.

sections.title: The ENABLE Command
sections.content:
The ENABLE command takes a list of capability names and requests the server to enable the named extensions. Once enabled, each extension remains active until the IMAP connection is closed. For each argument the server does one of three things. If the argument is not an extension known to the server, the server must ignore the argument. If it is an extension known to the server but not specifically permitted to be enabled using ENABLE, the server must also ignore the argument, because knowing about an extension does not necessarily imply supporting it. If the argument is an extension that is supported by the server and that needs to be enabled, the server must enable it for the duration of the connection. At present this applies only to CONDSTORE, and once an extension is enabled there is no way to disable it.

Clients should only include extensions that need to be enabled by the server. The ENABLE command is only valid in the authenticated state, before any mailbox is selected, and clients must not issue it once they have selected or examined a mailbox, though server implementations do not have to check that no mailbox was selected earlier in the connection.

The command can be issued multiple times in a session and is additive, so ENABLE a b followed by ENABLE c is the same as a single ENABLE a b c. When multiple ENABLE commands are issued, each corresponding ENABLED response should contain only the extensions enabled by that command. There are no limitations on pipelining ENABLE, so it is possible to send ENABLE and then immediately SELECT, or a LOGIN immediately followed by ENABLE.

The server must not change the capability list as a result of executing ENABLE. A capability command issued right after an ENABLE command must list the same capabilities as one issued before it.
sections.plainLanguage: The client sends a list of names and the server switches on the ones it supports and is allowed to switch on. Anything else in the list is quietly ignored. The command has to come after login and before the client opens a mailbox, and it can be repeated; each time, the server lists only what it turned on in that call.

sections.title: The ENABLED Response
sections.content:
If the ENABLE command is successful, the server must send an untagged ENABLED response. The ENABLED response occurs as a result of an ENABLE command, and its capability listing contains a space-separated listing of capability names that the server supports and that were successfully enabled.

The ENABLED response may contain no capabilities, which means that none of the extensions listed by the client were successfully enabled. The server's reply to the command itself is OK with the text Relevant capabilities enabled, or BAD with the text No arguments, or syntax error in an argument.
sections.plainLanguage: After the command the server sends an untagged line naming the extensions it turned on. If it turned none of them on, the line is empty, and the client can tell that from the response.

sections.title: Formal Syntax
sections.content:
The syntax is given in Augmented Backus-Naur Form, with the non-terminals capability and command-any defined in the base IMAP specification. Except as noted otherwise, all alphabetic characters are case-insensitive, and implementations must accept these strings in a case-insensitive fashion.

The capability rule adds the word ENABLE to the list of capabilities. The command-any rule adds ENABLE followed by one or more capability names separated by spaces. The response-data rule adds the untagged form, and enable-data defines the ENABLED response and its optional list of capability names.
sections.plainLanguage: The formal grammar adds one command name, one response name, and a list of extension names after each. The names are not case-sensitive.

sections.title: A Note to Extension Designers
sections.content: Designers of IMAP extensions are discouraged from creating extensions that require ENABLE unless there is no good alternative design. Extensions that cause potentially incompatible behavior changes to deployed server responses, and thus benefit from ENABLE, have a higher complexity cost than extensions that do not.
sections.plainLanguage: The authors of the RFC ask extension designers not to lean on this command. An extension that changes what the server sends, so that clients must be opted in, costs more to implement than one that does not.

sections.title: Security Considerations
sections.content: It is believed that this extension does not add any security considerations that are not already present in the base IMAP protocol.
sections.plainLanguage: The command adds nothing new in security terms beyond what the base IMAP protocol already has.

data.title: ABNF rules
data.code:
capability    =/ "ENABLE"

command-any   =/ "ENABLE" 1*(SP capability)

response-data =/ "*" SP enable-data CRLF

enable-data   = "ENABLED" *(SP capability)

viz.caption: WHAT THE SERVER DOES WITH EACH NAME IN THE LIST

items.title: Known but not permitted to be enabled
items.text: The server ignores the argument, because knowing an extension does not mean supporting it.

items.title: Supported and needs enabling
items.text: The server enables it for the rest of the connection. There is no way to turn it off again.
